idiom_name: struct { int32_t from, until; } of yyyymmdd ordinals + eff_contains()/eff_overlaps()
implementation_notes: C has no date type at all: <time.h> offers struct tm (tm_year counts from 1900, tm_mon is zero-based, fields normalised by mktime()) and time_t seconds since the Epoch, and converting a calendar date to time_t always goes through the local time zone - so a validity period built on time_t inherits zone and DST errors. The workable C realization is therefore to store the bounds as comparable, zone-free values (an int32 yyyymmdd or a day number) and to hand-write the two operations the pattern needs: eff_contains(period, day) and eff_overlaps(a, b). Classic struct tm/time_t code is still justified when the period is genuinely instant-based - a lease or session starting at a timestamp - and then compare time_t values with difftime() rather than subtracting them, keeping every value in one zone.
pitfalls: time_t is not a calendar date: mktime() interprets struct tm in local time and normalises out-of-range fields, so a "date" built that way changes meaning across zones and DST transitions - keep date-granularity periods as yyyymmdd ordinals.
The 0/negative sentinel for an open end must be handled in every operation; testing it in eff_contains() but forgetting it in eff_overlaps() makes open periods never overlap.
strftime/strptime formats are locale- and platform-dependent (%F is POSIX, not ISO C); parse the fixed YYYY-MM-DD form with sscanf or a small hand-written parser to stay portable.
